adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The conservation department received the leather-bound ledger in the spring, but the accession paperwork lagged for weeks. Its spine had cracked along the hinge, and the first and last gatherings were loose enough to shift when the volume was opened. The reading room was closed, so the work began on the long table near the north window, where the light was steady and the air was dry.

First, the conservator photographed every ruled page and recorded the condition of the ink. Iron gall had burned through in places, leaving small brown halos around the entries. The paper was not brittle, which surprised everyone who had handled similar ledgers from the same merchant house. The sewing cords were intact along the spine, and the boards had warped only slightly at the corners.

Cleaning came next. A soft brush took the loose dust from the gutter, and a smoke sponge lifted the soot that had settled along the top edge. The conservator worked from the center outward, watching the surface rather than the clock, because haste would have smeared the ink. The page edges were dusty, and the gutter was worse, but neither required washing.

The old repair along the hinge had to come away before anything else could be done. A poultice of methyl cellulose softened the wheat-starch paste, and the Japanese tissue lifted without tearing the original paper beneath. The residue came off with a swab and warm water, and the joint was left to dry under light weight for the rest of the afternoon.

Then came the mending of the torn leaves. The conservator chose a thin kozo paper that matched the tone of the ledger paper, tore narrow strips along the fibres, and laid them across the tears with a paste brush. Each strip overlapped the tear by only a little. Behind the first gathering, a previous owner had glued a strip of ordinary writing paper, which had darkened and stiffened over the decades.

The most delicate step was the infill of the losses at the spine fold. The conservator mixed 40 grams of wheat paste and brushed it onto the linen backing, then pressed the new lining into the fold with a bone folder. The paste had to be thin enough to soak the linen without bleeding into the paper. After the lining was smoothed, the volume was wrapped in blotting paper and left beneath a board weighted with a pair of bricks.

The color matching took the longest. The conservator prepared small samples of toned paper and held them against the original leaves near the window, rejecting several because they were too warm or too grey. The final choice was almost invisible from arm's length, which is the standard the department prefers. A note in the treatment file recorded the mixture and the supplier, so the work could be repeated if the ledger ever needed treatment again.

Sewing the gatherings back onto the cords was done on a small frame that the department had owned for years. The thread was linen, the needle was thick, and the stations were already marked from the original binding. The conservator kept the tension even and checked the alignment of the pages after each gathering, because a single loose station would throw the whole text block forward.

Finally, the boards were reattached with a hollow back, and the book was cased in with a new spine of toned calfskin. The gold tooling was not restored; the department decided to leave the worn lettering as it was found. A box was made to hold the volume, with a chemise of unbleached cotton and a label on the spine.

The ledger returned to the reading room on a Thursday. The curator opened it, turned to the index, and read the first entry aloud. The pages lay flat, the fold held, and the ink was still legible where the iron gall had not burned through. The treatment file was filed with the accession records, and the photographs were stored on the department server.
